Police sergeants George W. Lyons
and Daniel M. Kelleher, two of the
oldest members in the Police Depart
ment in point of service, and patrol
men Edward Abrahams, Harry Taylor,
John Ward and Carmine DiAlare, also
men with long and creditable records
as officers, were before the Board of
Police Commissioners yesterday after
noon, to answer to charges of neglect
of duty in failing to report that intoxicating
liquors were being sold by the
Olympia Athletic Club, at No. 505
Shipley street raided several Sundays ago.

The men pleaded not guilty, and
after going into the matter to some
extent the Police Commissioners con-
cluded to withhold their decision until
next Thursday afternoon. Former
State Senator Thomas M. Monaghan,
City Tax Collector Eugene N. Sayers
and Samuel S. Adams, an attorney,
were interested spectators.

President Charles R. Jones, of the
board, informed the men concerning
the charges against them and took
occasion to say that he termed the
Olympia Club case an aggravated one,
but not isolated and that the police
men on street duty had failed to do
their duty when they did not report
clubs where liquor was sold. He said
the weekly reports of the street ser-
geants might just as well be written
for a year in advance, so little did
they vary.

Mr. Jones said he was tired of being
stopped on the street every day and
told that this and that club was sell-
ing liquor on Sunday, and he made
the statement that a good detective
could buy liquor in 10 to 15 clubs next
Sunday. He said the Olympia Club
was nothing more than an open bar or
saloon and that boxing had been con-
ducted there under the guise of work-
outs.

Commissioner William Bowers
wanted to know why the officers of
the district did not know of these
things. He remarked that the
work done in this connection appears
to come from the chief of police and
the men under the head of the depart-
ment. We're not giving him their sup-
port.

The accused patrolmen, with the
exception of Patrolman Taylor, who
refused to make a statement, admitted
they knew of the existence of clubs in
their district, but did not know posi-
tively that liquor was being sold in
them. The men denied that they
knew more than they put in their
weekly reports, a charge made by Mr.
Jones. Patrolman Ward asked the
commissioners if it was not known by
common repute that clubs sell and
have sold for years intoxicating li-
quors to their members. The names
of some of the most prominent clubs
in the city were mentioned and Mr.
Bowers agreed that this was so, but
he thought the evidence, even against
them, could be gotten.

The entire situation was gone over
and thoroughly threshed out, even to
gambling, and the arrest of George H.
Simon, accused of running a book on
horse racing, the statement being
made by Chief of Police Black that at
least $500 a week is sent out of the
city daily in bets on the horses. Chief
Black said the gambling case was
worked up on information submitted
by Commissioner Thomas Stayton.

Chief Black said he had no personal
feeling in the matter and that his aim
was to secure more efficiency and a
good department. He spoke of the
policy playing that was prevalent here
some years ago and added that he did
not intend any one should weave a
rope around his neck.

Mr. Jones said that the chief was
entitled to the assistance of all the
men on the force and that he was not
the one whom the commission expect-
ed to go about the streets to obtain
evidence in cases. Chief Black said
he knew it was hard to get into some
clubs, but if the men came to him
with complaints he would see that
they got help. He advocated that the
men should work together and that one
should tell the other of what was go-
ing on so that the greatest good can be

WASHINGTON, Dec. 1.—Opponents of woman suffrage appeared before the House Rules Committee to-day to argue why a committee on woman suffrage should not be created by the House. The delegation was headed by Mrs. J. Dodge of New York, who yesterday was reelected president of the National Association opposed to woman suffrage. The delegation marched to the House office Building in a body. In that respect they followed the plan of the National American Woman suffrage Association which yesterday sent a delegation of nearly one thousand women to present the suffragist argument to the Rules Committee.

Speakers for the opponents declared working women were opposed to the franchise because they would lose more. They answered the statement of the suffragists that the women need the franchise and were strongly in favor of it.

The movement was sporadic in its nature and that the ballot was not wanted by many women as the suffragists declared. It was denied that the suffrage movement had grown to such proportions as to demand a House committee.

Suffragist sympathizers had been warned by Mrs. Anna Howard Shaw, president of their association, to remain away from the hearing room and give their undivided attention to the business of the suffrage convention which they had been sent as delegates.

Mr. Eley will admit that his reasoning above recited is not satisfactory answer.
